title: What It Takes to Hold It There: Gravity and the Motors

questions.question: A proportional controller is told to hold a 0.5 kg payload stretched out horizontally. Where does the tool end up?
options: Above it, from the integral term
About a third of a metre below it, because the torque gravity demands is the gain times the error, so the error cannot be zero
At the commanded pose, because the controller drives the error to zero
questions.explanation: Measured, 326.6 mm at a gain of 50 N m per radian. The controller supplies torque only in proportion to an error, so holding the arm needs one.

questions.question: Why is the sag zero when the arm points straight up?
options: The torque is the weight times the cosine of the angle to the horizontal, and the cosine of a right angle is zero
questions.explanation: The holding torque follows the horizontal distance of each weight from the joint. At vertical that distance is nothing, so no torque is needed and the sag is nothing.

questions.question: Why does the test compare the torque formula with the slope of the potential energy?
options: It shares no algebra with the formula
questions.explanation: The same mistake in both cannot pass; they agreed to 4.8e-09 N m over 507 poses. A check built from the same reasoning as the code can only confirm the reasoning. The energy slope is a different route to the same torque.

questions.question: Motors of 20 and 8 N m hold 0.776 kg stretched out and 2.283 kg with the elbow bent. What does a payload rating of 2.2 kg mean?
options: It is the rating of the arm
It is the average over the workspace
questions.explanation: True in the bent pose and nearly three times too high for the longest lever. The torque is a straight line in the payload with different coefficients at every pose, so each pose has its own heaviest payload.

questions.question: An arm standing upright is nudged and falls with a gain of 10 and holds with a gain of 50. What changed?
options: At the top gravity pushes the shoulder over by 17.6 N m per radian
Nothing physical; the simulation is noisy
questions.explanation: A gain below that cannot bring it back and one above can. Upright is a hilltop: the torque falls as the arm leans, so gravity adds to the lean. The gain has to exceed the slope.

questions.question: heaviest_payload compares with a tolerance when deciding that a joint never runs out, not with exactly zero. Why?
options: Doubles cannot be compared with zero
Zero is not a valid payload
questions.explanation: An exact comparison reports a payload in the millions for a pose that should have no limit. The pose is exactly upright in the mathematics and a rounding error away from it in the machine. A tolerance says what is meant.
